content.intro: Learn scheduled operations through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Scheduled Operations matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines scheduled operations as part of email, background work, and external services. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Periodic cleanup tasks; Scheduled notifications; Report generation; Expired-record handling; Monitoring scheduled-task failures. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Periodic cleanup tasks
items.text: Periodic cleanup tasks crosses an application boundary. Define the data contract, timeouts/failure behavior, authorization and retry/idempotency rules; verify with synthetic input and avoid live secrets in practice.

items.title: Expired-record handling
items.text: Expired-record handling affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: Monitoring scheduled-task failures
items.text: Treat Monitoring scheduled-task failures as a reproducible diagnostic: capture the exact input and observed result, isolate one hypothesis, and add a regression test once the cause is fixed. Avoid exposing internal stack traces or secrets to public users.
